extracted.intended_audience: actors, improvisers, improv teachers, theatre students, and comedy performers
extracted.subtask_description: Practical principles, exercises, and teaching heuristics for improvisation and theatrical spontaneity—covering status work, spontaneity, narrative skills, mask and trance work, and classroom games.

rubrics_metrics.name: Say Yes / Accept Offers (Don't Block)
rubrics_metrics.description: "Anything an actor does is an 'offer'. Each offer can either be accepted, or blocked." Good improvisers accept offers; saying yes and building on offers keeps scenes alive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Repeated advice and exercises (e.g., 'yes and' games) illustrate that accepting offers prevents paralysis and story-killing. Anti-pattern: blocking or negating another player's offer (saying 'no') which stalls the scene. Coaching note: reward and reinforce accepting responses in early practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lower the 'No-Saying' Intellect / Remove Ownership of Content
rubrics_metrics.description: "Switch off the no-saying intellect and welcome the unconscious as a friend..." and "You have to trick students into believing that the content isn't important and that it looks after itself."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Techniques include misdirection, constraints, and rituals that absolve participants of responsibility for content (e.g., prompts, forced-choice rules, counting tasks). Purpose: bypass cognitive censoring so first thoughts arise. Example: asking someone to write while they count backwards to distract the sensor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Status Awareness and Manipulation
rubrics_metrics.description: Johnstone's central claim: life and theatre are 'status transactions'—actors must perceive and manipulate relative status (high vs low) in every interaction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exercises: play a fractionally higher or lower status than your partner; practice minimal status shifts to make scenes authentic. Includes the 'ten golden rules' for Number Ones (leaders) and many anecdotes showing how status drives behavior. Use status work to internalize roles so actors stop thinking and 'just are' the role.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use Body Language to Signal Status
rubrics_metrics.description: Specific physical signals (space taken, eye contact, head stillness, posture, timing of syllables) convey status. For example: 'The more space you take up, the higher you put your status.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical manipulations: hold head still to increase perceived authority; breaking or holding eye contact alters status; use long vs short vowel endings as interruption signals. Train actors to notice and use these micro-behaviours deliberately.

rubrics_metrics.name: Create a Safe Space; Permit Failure
rubrics_metrics.description: Beginning improvisers must be protected from shame; teachers must make the space safe so actors will take risks and not self-censor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not punish odd or grotesque material; reassure participants that whatever arises will be accepted. Use group agreement, acceptance rituals, and explicit permission to fail. Pedagogical note: safety is a prerequisite for lowering filters and encouraging spontaneity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Don't Strive for Originality; Accept First Thoughts
rubrics_metrics.description: "An artist who is inspired is being obvious... Striving after originality takes you far away from your true self, and makes your work mediocre." The first idea is often the best for spontaneity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encourage performers to use their immediate, obvious responses rather than over-editing. Anti-pattern: asking for 'original' ideas which produces hesitation and mediocrity. Exercises: one-word story, forced quick-response tasks to reinforce first-thought acceptance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Narrative Skills: Prompting Questions & Listing Exercises
rubrics_metrics.description: Use rapid, simple questions and list exercises to elicit pre-existing story material and increase 'babble'—the uncensored flow of narrative thought.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: ask sensory/location questions ('what is the color of the book next to you?') to unlock stories; one-word-story chains; sequential vs non-sequential lists to explore associative vs non-associative thinking. These practices reveal that people often have stories already formed if prompted correctly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mask Work: Fuse the Actor to the Mask
rubrics_metrics.description: Mask exercises aim to make the actor 'be' the mask rather than 'act' the mask—building a distinct personality tied to the mask.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Procedure: start with mirror observation, move into embodied movement, give speech lessons as needed, and allow the mask to find its own behaviors and lines. Do not over-direct the mask's voice; allow consistent mask behaviors to emerge. Note: mask work can produce transformative, childlike behaviour and long-term imprinting of mask speech.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trance / Possession Techniques to Induce Spontaneity
rubrics_metrics.description: Drawing on examples of possession cults and trance rituals, Johnstone advocates methods that temporarily suspend normal constraints ('take the responsibility of action away') to permit more uninhibited behaviour.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Techniques include ritual, role-assumption, guided hallucinations, and contextual signals that license extreme behaviour. Use careful preparation and reintegration afterward (nursing actors back to normal). Purpose is to lower egoic censorship and access primary-state creativity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-Defense / Vulnerability as a Tool
rubrics_metrics.description: Displaying non-defensive vulnerability (e.g., exposing the neck/underbelly) can function as a social tactic to end conflict or shift dynamics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Teach actors to experiment with deliberate vulnerability in scenes to alter outcomes and status relations. Warning: recognize cultural and safety limits; non-defense is a tactical choice, not self-harm.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid Playing for Sympathy ('Playing Ill')
rubrics_metrics.description: Players who habitually 'play ill' or solicit sympathy (feeble starts, looking inadequate) use a ploy that usually guarantees failure and bores the group.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Coach performers to notice and stop sympathy-seeking postures. Swap these patterns for healthier status-play or honest offers that invite engagement rather than pity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use Short, Diverse Games to Build Skills
rubrics_metrics.description: A repertoire of quick, varied games develops different faculties: spontaneity, listening, status signalling, narrative speed, and group dynamics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Games cited include: one-word story, yes-and scenarios, swearing game, group simultaneous storytelling, object-feel-to-music, vowel/consonant answer constraints, random-sound exchanges, escalating multi-person rambling, and many situational prompts. Use games to give low-risk practice and to overload sensors so new behaviours emerge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Teaching Principle: Avoid Destructive Correction; Foster Talent
rubrics_metrics.description: "Many teachers think of children as immature adults... bad teachers are wrecking talent." Teachers should not 'correct' creativity into paralysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasize facilitation over judgement: lift students' confidence, avoid making first ideas 'wrong' through over-correction, and use positive reinforcement. Recognize the difference between constructive coaching and destructive training that extinguishes spontaneity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use Misdirection and Constraints to Bypass the Sensor
rubrics_metrics.description: Deliberate constraints or distracting tasks (e.g., counting backwards while performing) help bypass the censoring 'sensor' that inhibits spontaneity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design exercises where attention is split or responses are rule-bound (answer pattern based on vowel/consonant, forced rapid response) to force unconscious material into performance. Combine with reassurance so participants don't become ashamed of odd content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Centering/Character 'Centre' Exercises
rubrics_metrics.description: Imagining different centers in the body (abdomen, nose tip, eye, outside the body) produces distinct psychological and comic characters (earthy, curious, sly, cowardly, sharp).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use guided imagery to place an imagined 'centre' and observe resulting physicality and temperament. Employ these as quick character development tools in scene work and mask training.
